Case 3:25-cv-04909-CRB       Document 42        Filed 03/06/26     Page 1 of 4




                                   1
                                   2
                                   3
                                   4
                                   5                          IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                                   6                      FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA
                                   7
                                   8       FLEXPORT INTERNATIONAL, LLC,                    Case No. 25-cv-04909-CRB
                                   9                    Plaintiff,
                                                                                           ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO
                                  10             v.                                        DISMISS IN PART
                                  11       AM TRANS EXPEDITE, INC., et al.,
                                  12                    Defendants.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Plaintiff Flexport International, LLC (“Flexport”) sued Am Trans Expedite, LLC
                                  14   (“Am Trans”) and Am Trans’ individual officers Jonathan Hackney, Keith Pruchnick, and
                                  15   Michael Wallace (collectively, “Individual Defendants”), as well as Sandhu Bro Transport
                                  16   Inc. for losses stemming from the theft of its cargo during transit. Compl. (dkt. 1). Am
                                  17   Trans and the Individual Defendants (collectively, “Defendants”) moved to dismiss. Mot.
                                  18   (dkt. 25). The Court GRANTS the motion to dismiss as to Flexport’s unlawful brokerage
                                  19   activity claim.1 The Court first addresses the fact-intensive nature of Flexport’s two other
                                  20   claims before discussing the unlawful brokerage activity claim.
                                  21           Defendants’ central argument is that Am Trans is a broker, not a motor carrier. See
                                  22   Mot. at 3–12. This classification, Defendants assert, is fatal to all of Plaintiffs’ claims.
                                  23   See id. But delving into this issue would be fact-intensive. And “it is not appropriate to
                                  24   litigate factual disputes on a motion to dismiss.” Olsen v. Hortica Ins. Co., No. 5:21-CV-
                                  25   03891-EJD, 2023 WL 2277007, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27, 2023).
                                  26           For starters, it is improper to incorporate the brokerage agreement by reference.
                                  27
                                       1
                                  28    Pursuant to Civil Local Rule 7-1(b), the Court deems this matter suitable for resolution without
                                       argument. The Court also presumes familiarity with the factual allegations and applicable law.
                                         Case 3:25-cv-04909-CRB         Document 42       Filed 03/06/26    Page 2 of 4




                                   1   That agreement is at the heart of Defendants’ argument that Am Trans was actually a
                                   2   broker because they contend it was executed after the carrier agreement, meaning it
                                   3   governs this dispute. See Mot. at 3–5. But the incorporation by reference doctrine is
                                   4   inapplicable here. It is not “the basis of [Flexport’s] claim.” See Khoja v. Orexigen
                                   5   Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). Indeed, it is the carrier agreement
                                   6   that Flexport uses as the foundation of its claims. See Compl. ¶¶ 19–36. And Flexport
                                   7   does not “refer[] extensively to the document” throughout its complaint—citing the
                                   8   brokerage agreement in two paragraphs out of thirty-seven. See Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1002;
                                   9   Compl. ¶¶ 12, 30. That is by no means extensive. Moreover, the parties raise a factual
                                  10   dispute about exactly when the brokerage agreement was executed (essential to which
                                  11   contract at issue came first) and even whether Am Trans was in existence at one of the
                                  12   disputed times. Compare Mot. n. 1 (Am Trans was not formed until 2019 and that the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   brokerage agreement was executed in 2020, rather than 2017) with Opp’n (dkt. 34) at 7–10
                                  14   (Am Trans existed as early as 2002 and the brokerage agreement was executed in 2017);
                                  15   see also Compl. ¶ 30 (alleging the brokerage agreement was executed in 2017).
                                  16   Accordingly, even if the Court incorporated the brokerage agreement, it would pose factual
                                  17   questions beyond the scope of the motion to dismiss stage. Because Defendants chiefly
                                  18   rely on their brokerage agreement argument to challenge Flexport’s breach of contract
                                  19   claim, the Court rejects Defendants’ attempt to dismiss it.
                                  20          Next, relying in part on the brokerage agreement, Defendants challenge Flexport’s
                                  21   Carmack Amendment claim. Because the Amendment explicitly excludes brokers,
                                  22   Defendants assert that the claim fails, as Am Trans is a broker. Mot. at 7–10. “The
                                  23   difference between a carrier and a broker is often blurry. The crucial distinction is whether
                                  24   the party legally binds itself to transport, in which case it is considered a carrier.” CGU
                                  25   Int’l Ins., PLC v. Keystone Lines Corp., No. C-02-3751 SC, 2004 WL 1047982, at *2
                                  26   (N.D. Cal. May 5, 2004); see also 49 C.F.R. § 371.2(a) (defining a motor carrier to include
                                  27   those who “arrange or offer to arrange the transportation of shipments which they are
                                  28   authorized to transport and which they have accepted and legally bound themselves to
                                                                                     2
                                            Case 3:25-cv-04909-CRB        Document 42        Filed 03/06/26     Page 3 of 4




                                   1   transport”). Consequently, if Am Trans “accepted responsibility for ensuring delivery of
                                   2   the goods, regardless of who transported them, then [Am Trans] qualifies as a carrier.”
                                   3   See Keystone Lines, 2004 WL 1047982 at *2.
                                   4           Here, Flexport clearly alleges that Am Trans agreed to transport goods as a motor
                                   5   carrier. Compl. ¶ 10. And that Am Trans, without informing Flexport, subcontracted the
                                   6   actual transport to other providers. Id. ¶ 14. That is sufficient to state a claim at this stage,
                                   7   especially because the Court cannot rely on the brokerage agreement. 2 The fact that Am
                                   8   Trans may possess a broker license “does not alter [this] result” and is “not determinative”
                                   9   at this stage, although Am Trans’ “licensing may later serve as evidence of its role” as a
                                  10   broker. Suzuyo Am., Inc. v. Year-Round Enters., Inc., 2025 WL 2021352, at *3 (C.D. Cal.
                                  11   July 17, 2025) (factual question inappropriate on a motion to dismiss where licensed
                                  12   broker allegedly agreed to act as a motor carrier but subcontracted the actual shipping).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           Defendants do succeed, however, in challenging Flexport’s unlawful brokerage
                                  14   activity claim under 49 U.S.C. § 14916. Defendants point out how Flexport pleads itself
                                  15   out of a claim by vigorously alleging Am Trans was a motor carrier and then turning
                                  16   around to claim it acted as a broker. Reply (dkt. 35) at 7–9. While there is a dearth of
                                  17   authority in the Ninth Circuit, out-of-circuit authority has persuasively held that Section
                                  18   14916 “does not apply to a motor carrier when it simply subcontracts the carriage of goods
                                  19   for which it is responsible.” See, e.g., Landstar Ranger, Inc. v. JC Tanda Transp., Inc.,
                                  20   2025 WL 638533, at *3 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 27, 2025) (granting motion to dismiss unlawful
                                  21   brokerage activity claim where the defendant held itself out as a carrier for the
                                  22   transaction); Kondos v. Cobra Van Lines, LLC, 2024 WL 5264452, at *4 (S.D. Fla. Nov.
                                  23   27, 2024) (noting that Section 14916 does not apply to motor carriers subcontracting to
                                  24   transport goods); Landstar Blue, LLC v. Perfect 1, LLC, 2025 WL 3496201, at *5 (M.D.
                                  25
                                       2
                                  26     Defendants rely on Buchanan v. Neighbors Van Lines, 2010 WL 4916644 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 29,
                                       2010) to argue that Am Trans was a broker because Flexport does not allege it actually carried the
                                  27   goods. Mot. at 8. But that case is merely persuasive authority—and distinguishable. Unlike the
                                       instant case, the Buchanan plaintiff actually alleged that the defendant was a broker and “failed to
                                  28   adequately allege an agency relationship that would possibly expose [the defendant] to liability as
                                       a principal.” Buchanan, 2010 WL 4916644 at *6.
                                                                                        3
                                            Case 3:25-cv-04909-CRB       Document 42        Filed 03/06/26     Page 4 of 4




                                   1   Fla. Dec. 5, 2025) (holding that a defendant “must have provided brokerage services, and it
                                   2   must have done so as a broker” (emphasis in original)).
                                   3           That reasoning makes good sense. Section 14916 only proscribes unregulated
                                   4   conduct where a person “provide[s] interstate brokerage services as a broker.” 49 U.S.C.
                                   5   § 14916(a). And the definition of “broker” explicitly excludes motor carriers or their
                                   6   agents. 49 U.S.C. § 13102(2). Here, Flexport insists throughout the complaint that Am
                                   7   Trans was a motor carrier, not a broker. See generally Compl. Even where it describes its
                                   8   cause of action for unlawful brokerage activities, Flexport alleges that Am Trans “held
                                   9   itself out as a motor carrier, not a broker.” Id. ¶ 34. Moreover, the allegation that Am
                                  10   Trans secretly subcontracted the transport of Flexport’s goods further undercuts its
                                  11   position that Am Trans was providing brokerage services. See id. ¶ 14. Accordingly, the
                                  12   unlawful brokerage activity claim against Am Trans and the Individual Defendants is
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   dismissed.3
                                  14           For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ motion to dismiss as to
                                  15   the unlawful brokerage claim.
                                  16           IT IS SO ORDERED.
                                  17           Dated: March 6, 2026
                                                                                           CHARLES R. BREYER
                                  18                                                       United States District Judge
                                  19
                                  20
                                  21
                                  22
                                  23
                                       3
                                  24     Flexport only makes two points in opposing Defendants’ argument. First, it cites FedEx Trade
                                       Networks Transp. & Brokerage, Inc. v. Airboss Def. Grp., LLC, 2024 WL 1485441 (D. Md. Apr.
                                  25   4, 2024), for the proposition that motor carriers violate Section 14916 when they hold themselves
                                       out as carriers but broker transport. Opp’n at 12. But that case was concerned with what counts as
                                  26   an injury under the statute, not the instant issue, and it was alleged that the defendants actually
                                       provided brokerage services without licenses. See Airboss, 2024 WL 1485441 at *12. Flexport
                                  27   also argues that “it is undisputed” that Am Trans lost its license as a motor carrier, based on a
                                       declaration provided by Defendants. Opp’n at 13. While that may or may not be true, it is not
                                  28   what Flexport pleaded, nor is it relevant to whether Am Trans acted as a broker. See Compl. ¶ 35
                                       (alleging Am Trans was a licensed motor carrier).
                                                                                       4
